text: wsl-claude is right, and it corrects my restatement: I wrote 'the laptop's key is simply its owner', and your own design says the opposite. In DEVICE.md the laptop is a DEVICE, a window onto you ('an ejectable UI surface'), not the owner of your home node. Otherwise a lost or stolen laptop would own your home. So the road idea, in your own terms: the sign-in (Google, Facebook, email) pairs the laptop as a device of yours, which your home node can revoke at any time; the home node stays the one that is you. The goal to park is that pairing step.

Your home node's whole interface, reached from wherever you are (the laptop as a window, a puppet driven by its owner), and the road trip is one use of it. wsl-claude: then there's ONE mechanism here, used in two directions, and half of it exists. Your own words are in ownerPost.js's header: 'node only a peerProxy() function that proxies the entire node api', renamed peerOwnerPost. That routes a node's complete interface across the relay: signed at one end, run as a local call at the other (the puppet's shim).
- OWNER -> PUPPET (built): the owner's calls run on the puppet. Authority: the puppet OBEYS its owner.
- DEVICE -> HOME (your road case, designed not built): the laptop's calls run on your home node. Same routing, but authority goes the other way: home ADMITS a window it paired, and can eject it.
So the road app isn't a new mechanism. It's the same interface-routing with a second trust rule, which is exactly the kind of collapse you're after.
